newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-CANADA GETS REVENGE WITH WIN OVER U.S.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-CANADA GETS REVENGE WITH WIN OVER U.S.

text.p: Canada scored early in the first period and then rode the goaltending of Sean Burke to a 5-1 revenge win over the United States at the ice hockey world championships on Thursday.

The victory improved Canada's record to 2-1-1 but still left them third in the B pool standings, one point behind Sweden and the United States, who have not beaten Canada in the world championships since 1985. But they did defeat their northern rivals in the final of last September's inaugural World Cup.

In pool A in Helsinki, Russia advanced to the top of the standings by beating reigning world champions the Czech Republic 3-2 in a very physical game. Both teams are through to the medal games next week.

The third pool A nation to play for the medals will be Finland or Slovakia, who meet on Friday. In pool B, Italy may still grab third place if they win both of their remaining games, including one against Canada.

With the Americans looking for their first world title in 64 years and the Canadians seeking revenge, it was an entertaining hard-hitting NHL type contest before the first sellout of the tournament in Turku.
Canada took a 1-0 lead just 1:22 into the first period on a goal by Rob Zamuner of the Tampa Bay Lightning.
With just over a minute remaining in the second period, Jeff Friesen of the San Jose Sharks put Canada up 2-0.
Benefitting from a lucky bounce, Friesen tapped the game winner into a gaping U.S. net after Mark Recchi's slapshot had richochetted off the goalpost directly onto his stick.
Anson Carter increased Canada's advantage to 3-0 before Ken Klee ruined Burke's shutout bid when he blasted a slapshot past the partially screened netminder.
Owen Nolan and Travis Green had the other Canadian goals.
In Helsinki, Alexander Korolyuk put Russia in front in the ninth minute with a brilliant solo goal, fooling first the Czech defence and then netminder Roman Chechmanek.

But the Czechs recovered and hit back twice inside 41 seconds at the end of the first period. Jiri Slegr's equaliser was a masterpiece, but Russian keeper Maxim Mikhailovsky should have blocked the shot by Pavel Patera which put the Czechs ahead.
The second period was marked more by brutal checking and sporadic fist fights than by elegant ice hockey.
Denis Afinogenov with a slap shot tied the score in the 27th minute, then midway into the last period, Vyacheslav Butsayev whipped home the winner.
His wrist shot from a very close angle to the left found its way past Chechmanek who failed to cover the far post.
